title: Coding Agents
summary: How AI agents read, write and run code in a loop, and how to get reliable work from them.

lessons.title: How coding agents work

concept.text:
A chatbot answers once. An agent works toward a goal in a loop: it decides on an action, uses a tool, looks at the result, and decides again, until the job is done.

A coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor's agent mode or GitHub Copilot's agent is an LLM connected to a small set of tools: read a file, search the codebase, edit a file, run a shell command. It finds the relevant code, makes a change, runs the tests, reads the failure, and fixes it, without you copying and pasting between windows.
concept.analogy: A chatbot is a consultant on the phone: they give advice and you do the work. An agent is a contractor on site with their own tools: they look around, do the work, check it, and call you over when a decision is needed.

visual.caption: The agent loop. It runs until the task is done or the agent needs you.

steps.title: Gather context
steps.text: The agent cannot see your whole project at once. It searches and reads files to build a picture, like a new developer exploring a codebase.

steps.title: Take action
steps.text: It edits files and runs commands through tools. Each tool result is appended to its context window.

steps.title: Verify
steps.text: Good agents run tests, type-checkers and linters, then read the output. Verification is what turns plausible code into working code.

steps.title: Stay within permissions
steps.text: You control what the agent may do without asking: read-only, edit files, or run commands. Risky actions prompt for approval.

interactive.prompt: An agent is asked to fix a bug. Order its actions.
items: Read the bug report and restate the goal
Search the codebase for the relevant function
Read the file and the failing test
Edit the code to fix the bug
Read the test output and fix anything still failing

challenge.prompt: An agent working on a long task starts repeating earlier mistakes and forgetting instructions from the start of the session. What is the most likely cause, and what can you do about it?
challenge.hint: Every file read and every command output takes up space somewhere finite.
challenge.solution: The **context window** is filling up. Every tool result is added to it, and when it is nearly full, older material gets summarised or dropped. Fixes: start a fresh session for a new task; keep durable instructions in a project memory file such as `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` that is loaded every time; break the work into smaller tasks; and have the agent write its plan and progress to a file it can re-read.

takeaways: An agent is an LLM in a loop with tools: think, act, observe, repeat.
Coding agents explore the codebase, edit files and run commands to verify their work.
The context window is the agent's working memory, and it is finite.

lessons.title: Using coding agents effectively

concept.text:
An agent amplifies how clearly you can describe what you want and how well you can check the result. The developers who get the most from agents treat them like a capable teammate: they give context, agree a plan before big changes, provide a way to verify, and review the output.

You remain responsible for the code. Read the diff before you accept it.
concept.analogy: Delegating to an agent is like delegating to a talented new hire. 'Make the app better' wastes a day. A ticket with the goal, the constraints, the relevant files and a definition of done gets shipped.

visual.caption: A reliable workflow for any non-trivial task.

nodes.label: Explore
nodes.detail: Have it read the code first

steps.title: Write a real brief
steps.text: State the goal, the constraints and what done looks like.
steps.code:
Weak:   fix the login bug

Strong: Users are logged out after 5 minutes instead of 24 hours.
        The session code is in src/auth/session.ts.
        Find the cause, fix it, and add a test that fails
        before the fix and passes after. Don't change the API.

steps.title: Give it a way to check itself
steps.text: Tests, a build command or a screenshot to match. An agent that can verify will iterate until it is right.

steps.title: Set up project memory
steps.text: A file such as `CLAUDE.md` holds the things you would tell any new developer: how to run tests, code style, and what never to touch.

steps.title: Commit often and course-correct early
steps.text: Commit working states so you can roll back. If the agent heads the wrong way, stop it and redirect instead of letting errors pile up.

questions.q: Which gives an agent the best chance of producing correct code?
options: A way to verify its work, such as tests
questions.explain: With feedback from tests, the agent can find and fix its own mistakes.

questions.q: Before a large refactor, what should you ask the agent to do first?
options: Explore the code and propose a plan for review
questions.explain: Catching a wrong approach at the plan stage is far cheaper than after 30 file edits.

questions.q: Who is responsible for code an agent wrote and you merged?
questions.explain: You own what you ship. Review it like any other pull request.

challenge.prompt: Rewrite this request so a coding agent can succeed first time: **'Add dark mode.'**
challenge.hint: Where is the styling? How is the preference chosen and remembered? How will you both know it works?
challenge.solution: "Add a dark mode to this React + Tailwind app. First read `src/index.css` and `App.jsx` and tell me your plan. Requirements: a toggle button in the header; default to the operating system preference; save the choice in localStorage; all text must keep at least 4.5:1 contrast in both themes. Use CSS variables for colours instead of hard-coding them per component. When finished, run `npm run build` and confirm it passes, then list the files you changed."

takeaways: Explore, plan, implement, verify, review: in that order.
Specific briefs and a way to verify matter more than clever wording.
Keep project knowledge in a memory file and commit often.
